transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I suppose I'm here because things got a little out of hand lately. I took on the historical society project, and I just felt like I could run the entire fundraiser myself, honestly. I started drawing up all these new quilt designs for it. Which reminds me, my grandmother used to make the most beautiful quilts. She had one of those old cast-iron pedal sewing machines. I actually saw one exactly like it at the antique mall last Tuesday when I was in there looking for a brass teapot. They wanted way too much for it, though. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, the fundraiser. Right. So I was calling all the volunteers and making these incredibly detailed schedules, just promising all these deadlines I couldn't possibly meet. And getting people to commit on the phone is just impossible these days. I called Susan to help, and she just went on and on about her daughter's wedding in Ohio. Can you imagine having a February wedding in Ohio? The snow must be an absolute nightmare for the guests driving in. But yes, the historical society... I guess I just bit off more than I could chew.
During this time, were you needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling full of energy?

Well, yes, for a while there I was hardly sleeping at all. Maybe two or three hours a night? And I'd pop right out of bed, completely ready to start sewing or making my phone calls. I actually called my sister Martha at 4:30 in the morning once because I had this brilliant idea for the quilt backing. She was furious, of course. Martha has always been so particular about her sleep, especially since she bought one of those fancy memory foam mattresses. You know, I read that those things off-gas terrible chemicals. I saw an article about it in a magazine at the dentist's office. Dr. Evans, he just retired last month, which is a real shame because he was so gentle with the novocaine... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, my sleep. Yes, I had all that energy then. But lately it's completely different. Now I either just lie awake in the dark worrying about every little thing, or I end up sleeping way too late and I still feel completely worn out when I finally drag myself up.
During that high-energy time, did you ever hear or see things that other people couldn’t?

No, no, nothing like that. I've always had a very vivid imagination, but I wasn't seeing things that weren't there. Although, speaking of seeing things, the other day I was looking out my kitchen window and I saw the strangest bird at my feeder. It had this bright blue patch on its wing, and I've been trying to figure out what it was. I have this wonderful old bird-watching book that belonged to my uncle Arthur. He was an avid bird watcher, you know. He used to take me out to the state park when I was a little girl with his big heavy binoculars. They had leather straps that smelled just like saddle soap. I love the smell of saddle soap, it reminds me of the tack room at the stable where my daughter used to take riding lessons... 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, seeing things. No, I wasn't hallucinating or anything like that. Just regular things, like that bird.
During that high-energy time, were you hospitalized because of your behavior?

Hospitalized? Oh heavens, no. I've never had to go to the hospital for anything like that. I mean, the last time I was in a hospital was when my husband had his gallbladder out a few years back. That was over at Mercy General, and let me tell you, the cafeteria food there is just abysmal. They gave him this green Jell-O that looked like it had been sitting out since the Reagan administration. I actually tried to bring him some homemade chicken soup in a thermos to make up for it. 

It was my mother's recipe—she always swore by adding a little parsnip to the broth. Parsnips give it this wonderful earthy sweetness, you know? You can't really find good parsnips at the regular grocery store anymore, though. You have to go to the farmer's market on Saturday mornings, and parking down there is just an absolute nightmare ever since they started letting that local bluegrass band set up right next to the tomato stands. I love music, but the banjo is just so loud when you're trying to count your change... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, the hospital. Right. No, I wasn't in the hospital during all that fundraiser business. I was just at home, running myself ragged.
During that high-energy time, did your behavior cause serious problems at work, socially, or financially?

Well, yes, I suppose it did cause some problems. I mean, my husband has had to take over all the household routines lately. And he's had to deal with the historical society for me because I just completely stopped keeping my commitments there. I couldn't even face the people waiting on me. Which is a shame, really, because we were right in the middle of planning the annual bake sale. 

I usually make my famous lemon pound cake for it. It's an old recipe, uses real butter and a whole cup of sour cream. The sour cream is the secret, it makes it so moist. I buy my sour cream from that little dairy farm out on Route 9. The couple who runs it, the Millers, they've been there for forty years. Mrs. Miller has the most beautiful garden, just overflowing with hydrangeas. I tried to grow hydrangeas once, but the soil here is too alkaline, so they always turned out pink instead of that lovely deep blue. I read somewhere that you can put coffee grounds in the soil to change the acidity. My husband drinks so much coffee, I don't know how he sleeps. He likes that dark French roast, the kind that smells almost burnt...

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, right, problems. Yes, I just couldn't face anyone, so he had to step in and handle everything with the house and the society.
About that high-energy period, did it last a full week or longer?

A week? Oh, goodness, it was much longer than a week. That whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months before everything finally fell apart. 

Five whole months. It started right around the time I was putting in my spring bulbs. I always plant the King Alfred daffodils, you know, the ones with the really big, bright yellow trumpets? I order them from this wonderful catalog that comes all the way from Holland. Though, getting packages delivered here has been such a headache lately. Our regular mail carrier retired—Bill was his name, such a sweet man, always had a milk bone in his pocket for the neighborhood dogs—and the new fellow just can't seem to read the house numbers right. 

Just last Tuesday he left my neighbor's electric bill in my box. I had to walk it over to Mrs. Gable, and she kept me on her porch for nearly an hour talking about her grandson's new braces. Those metal wires look so terribly painful, don't they? I remember when my daughter had braces, she could only eat mashed potatoes for days after getting them tightened. I used to make them from scratch with a little bit of roasted garlic and cream cheese. The cream cheese makes them so fluffy... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what were you asking me? Oh, the time. Yes, it wasn't a week. It was about five months of running on that high energy before the bottom just dropped out.
During that five-month high-energy period, were you doing much more activity than usual—like starting lots of projects or staying constantly busy?

Activity? Oh, my, yes. I was constantly moving. I had so much energy I couldn't even sit through a single television show with my husband. We usually watch those British murder mysteries together on PBS, you know the ones? The scenery is always so lovely, all those thatched-roof cottages and rolling green hills. I've always wanted to visit the Cotswolds. My sister went there for her 40th anniversary and she brought me back this beautiful wool blanket. It's so warm, but a little scratchy, to be honest. I usually have to put a cotton sheet under it if I'm going to use it on the sofa. 

Anyway, I couldn't sit still for even a minute of those shows. I'd be jumping up to measure fabric for the historical society banners, or writing down lists of things we needed, or just completely rearranging my craft supplies. Did you know they make these wonderful clear plastic bins now that stack perfectly? I bought a whole set of them at that big container store out by the mall. The traffic out there is just dreadful, though. They've been doing construction on the overpass for what feels like three years. I don't understand why they can't just finish it. The detour takes you right past the old paper mill, and the smell on a hot day is just... well, it's not pleasant. 

But yes, I'm sorry, I was just constantly busy. I couldn't just sit and be still, I had to be up doing things, measuring and organizing and writing notes.
After that five-month high-energy period ended, did you go through a period of feeling depressed most of the day nearly every day?

Well, yes, unfortunately. After everything just sort of fell apart with the historical society—you know, the orders for the banners fell behind and there were all those awful conflicts with the other volunteers—I just crashed. I've been stuck in this terrible, low, guilty place for about nine months now. 

Nine months... it feels like forever. My daughter's first pregnancy felt that long, of course. She had such terrible morning sickness with little Tommy. She couldn't keep anything down but saltines and ginger ale for the first trimester. I tried to make her some ginger tea from scratch, using real ginger root. You have to peel it with a spoon, did you know that? It works much better than a knife because it gets around all those little knobby parts. I buy my ginger at the international market downtown. They have the most fascinating produce section. Last time I was there, I saw this spiky fruit—a rambutan, I think it was called? It looked like a little red sea urchin. I didn't buy it, though. I'm not very adventurous with my fruit. I usually just stick to apples. Honeycrisp, mostly. They're so expensive, but they have that wonderful crunch. The ones at the regular grocery store always seem a bit mealy, don't they? 

Oh, I'm sorry, I lost my train of thought again. Yes, ever since the volunteer thing blew up, I've just been depressed and feeling guilty every single day for the last nine months.
